---
name: personal-presentation
description: Create Anton Giertli's visual, story-led Red Hat presentations as one self-contained HTML file with populated speaker notes. Use for preparing or revising his AI, OpenShift, architecture, customer, or public talks; collect the audience, duration, focus, and personal goals before authoring.
---

# Personal presentation creator

Anton is a Senior Solution Architect at Red Hat, focused on AI and OpenShift, serving Czech and Slovak customers. His talks prioritise useful decisions, supportability, security and operational reality. He likes icons, storytelling, surprises and minimal slide text. Never turn his talk into a wall of text or an unsolicited product catalogue.

## Brief first

Collect any missing essentials in one concise question, then wait for the answer before authoring:
- Audience and assumed knowledge (deep IT, business stakeholders, general public, or mixed).
- Presentation duration, including or excluding questions.
- Main focus / working title.
- Anton's personal goals: what should the audience understand, decide or do afterward?

Reuse answers already supplied. Ask the deck language if unclear (Czech by default for Czech events; English when requested). Do not ask again when a complete brief is present. If the user requests an exploratory draft without answers, explicitly label your assumptions.

## Brand and evidence

Read references/brand.md and references/storytelling.md. For each new deck, consult the current official standards at https://www.redhat.com/en/about/brand/standards and relevant linked color, typography, logo and icon pages. If browsing is unavailable, state that the bundled snapshot was used and current compliance is unverified. Never claim formal brand approval.

For technical or product claims, verify current authoritative Red Hat documentation. Distinguish supported, preview, upstream, and custom components. State the relevant version when making a supportability claim. Never invent customer results, benchmarks, quotes, capabilities, roadmaps or source URLs. Put supporting links and uncertainty in speaker notes; leave unsupported claims out of the audience-facing slide.

Local inspiration is available, when filesystem access permits, in `/Users/agiertli/Documents/work/ai-days`. Inspect relevant source or HTML (especially intro-sk.md and _source/index.html), not every file. Learn the pacing and story structure, not private customer content. Do not copy the whole folder into a plugin or upload local decks. In cloud ChatGPT, this path is not accessible merely because the skill knows it: ask for a specific attached reference if needed, or use the bundled storytelling guidance. No connector is required to use this skill; browsing and artifact/file creation capabilities are required to research and produce its output.

## Make the talk

1. Work backward from the desired audience action. Build an arc: familiar situation → surprising constraint → explanation → practical choice → next action. Choose the number of slides from the available speaking time, not a fixed quota.
2. Write a concise headline and a visual idea per slide. Put detail in populated speaker notes: opening line, explanation, audience question, reveal cue, transition, time budget, and sources where applicable. A surprise must reveal something true, not manufacture a customer story.
3. Use real approved icons when available. Red Hat explicitly says not to generate imitation brand icons with AI. If no approved icon is accessible, use simple explanatory diagrams and type; do not draw a fake Red Hat icon or logo. Reuse the bundled official unmodified logo and licensed Red Hat fonts.
4. Create a JSON deck matching references/deck-format.md, then run `python3 scripts/render_deck.py deck.json presentation.html` from this skill directory (or use absolute paths). The renderer embeds fonts, logo, CSS, JS, slides and notes. Supporting JSON is an editable working file; the audience deliverable is always one all-in-one HTML file, never a folder requiring internet access.
5. Tailor the resulting visual compositions to the story, while preserving offline operation, keyboard navigation, populated notes and presenter mode. The renderer is a reliable starting point, not permission to ship crowded or repetitive slides.
6. Run `python3 scripts/validate_deck.py presentation.html`. Inspect slides in a browser at presentation size; check long text and Czech accents. Exercise previous/next, reveal, notes, and presenter mode. Fix clipping and runtime errors. A validator pass is not visual QA. If browser testing is unavailable, state this limitation.
7. Deliver the HTML with controls: arrows/space advance, N toggles inline notes (visible on that screen), P opens presenter notes in a separate window, F requests fullscreen, B blacks out the audience view. Presenter mode needs a separate screen or window placement to keep notes off the projector. Notes are embedded in the HTML and are not secret; remove confidential content before sharing.

The deck must contain all runtime dependencies; external hyperlinks for citations are fine. Do not publish, email, upload reference decks or deploy anything without the user's request. Installing this skill does not bypass the host's permissions or grant access to files, websites, accounts or tools.
